title: The white days
hook: three days in the middle of each lunar month

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mondays and Thursdays, and your line: two days a week. Did either day pass with a thought of the fast? Day one thousand one hundred twelve.

Go outside on the right night of the month and the street is lit without a single lamp. The moon is full, or close to it, and the whole sky is pale. Islam keeps its calendar by that same moon. Each month begins with a thin crescent, swells to a round white face in the middle, and thins away again. And right there, at the bright middle of every month, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ pointed his companions to three days of fasting. Not a month, like Ramadan. Not two days every week, like yesterday. Three days, once a month, when the nights are at their brightest. Today, the white days.
screen: `A STREET LIT BY THE MOON.` → `A CALENDAR KEPT BY THE MOON.` → `THREE DAYS AT THE BRIGHT MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: First, the habit itself. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Abu Hurayrah says his close friend, meaning the Prophet, advised him to keep three things: fasting three days of every month, two units of prayer in the morning, and the witr prayer before sleep. Three days a month. A small, steady thing, handed to one person as a piece of friendly advice. Second, which three. A report in the collection of al-Tirmidhi has the Prophet telling Abu Dharr that if he fasts three days of a month, let it be the thirteenth, the fourteenth and the fifteenth. Those are the middle days of a lunar month, the days around the full moon. Tradition calls them the white days, and tradition says the name comes from the nights: white with moonlight from dusk to dawn. Third, why three. Another hadith in Bukhari, from the conversation with Abdullah ibn Amr that we'll meet tomorrow, says each good deed is counted ten times over, so fasting three days a month is like fasting all the time. The point isn't arithmetic. It's that something small and regular is treated as something large. Fourth, how people keep it. Because the dates follow the moon, the white days move against the calendar on the wall. Some Muslims check a lunar calendar each month, or an app, or the mosque's notice board, and mark the thirteenth to the fifteenth. Some fast all three, some one or two. It's voluntary, and nobody is blamed for missing it. The white days are simply there, every month, for anyone who wants them.
screen: `ADVICE FROM A FRIEND: THREE DAYS A MONTH.` · `THE THIRTEENTH, FOURTEENTH, FIFTEENTH.` · `SMALL AND REGULAR, COUNTED LARGE.` · `THE DATES MOVE WITH THE MOON.`

segments.voice: The practice: plan the white days, quietly, in your head. Settle, and let your breathing slow. Picture the moon as you last saw it. Was it thin, half, or round? You don't need to know the date. Just ask: when it's round next, where will I be? At work, at home, traveling? If you're Muslim and you fast, you might choose one of those three days to try. If not, you might choose one of those nights simply to step outside and look up. Hold that plan lightly. The bell holds the time.
The white days. The thirteenth, fourteenth and fifteenth of each lunar month, around the full moon, kept by some Muslims as three voluntary fasts. Today's word.
Your line: the full-moon days. Tonight, find the moon if you can, and see how far it is from round. Tomorrow: the fast of Dawud. Day one thousand one hundred twelve.

notes: Bukhari 1981 (Abu Hurayrah's three pieces of advice): confirm number.
Tirmidhi 761 (Abu Dharr told 13th, 14th, 15th): confirm number and grading; the same report is also in al-Nasa'i.
Bukhari 1976 (three days a month equal to a whole month, from the Abdullah ibn Amr conversation): confirm number and that the 'ten times' reasoning is in that report.
Explanation of the name 'white' (moonlit nights) is given as tradition, not as a sourced etymology; a Keeper may note the other explanation some scholars give.
Original: confirm الأيام البيض and the note that bid is the plural of abyad.

Editor: Bukhari 1976 says three days a month is 'like fasting all the time', not 'a whole month'; teach corrected. Name explanation recast as 'tradition says' (no 'usually explained'); word segment says 'around the full moon', since the 13th is not full.
